unit.title: Undertake fabrication, forming, bending and shaping

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What should you do first, before starting a fabrication job?
options: Cut all the material to rough size so that time is saved later
Tack the parts together loosely to see how they might fit
Read the drawing and check the sizes, materials and quantities
Order extra material in case some of it is spoiled

questions.stem: What is a cutting list?
options: A list of every part, with its size, material and number needed
A list of the cutting tools and blades kept in the tool store
A list of the mistakes made on the last job, so they are not repeated
A list of the machines that need new blades or repairs

questions.stem: What is the main danger at the front of a guillotine (power shear)?
options: Sparks from the blade flying into the eyes of the operator
Fingers crushed by the hold-downs or cut off by the blade
The sheet catching fire from the heat of the cutting blade
An electric shock through the sheet from the machine frame

questions.stem: Two people are feeding a large sheet into a guillotine. Who should work the foot pedal?
options: Both people, taking turns one after the other
Whoever is standing nearest to the pedal at the time
Anyone at all, as long as they shout a warning first
One person only, who can see both people's hands are clear

questions.stem: Why should leather or cut-resistant gloves be worn when handling sheet metal?
options: Sheet edges and burrs are sharp and can cut deeply
Gloves keep the sheet free from rust and fingerprints for painting
Gloves stop static electricity building up in the sheet
Gloves make the sheet easier to bend by hand

questions.stem: What is the main danger when using bending rolls?
options: The rolls get very hot and burn the hands of the operator
Oil from the rolls makes the plate rust quickly
Hands or clothing being drawn into the nip between the rolls
Sparks thrown from the rolls as the plate is formed

questions.stem: How should a long, heavy steel section be moved by hand?
options: By one person dragging it along the floor by one end
By one person carrying it balanced on one shoulder
By rolling it over loose pipes on the floor and pushing
By two or more people lifting together on a signal

questions.stem: When using a press brake, where must your hands be when the top tool comes down?
options: Holding the sheet close to the bend line so it stays straight
Well clear of the tools, holding the sheet by its outer edges
Under the sheet near the die, to support it as it bends
On top of the die, so you can feel the bend forming

questions.stem: Why should bends be made across the grain (rolling direction) of the sheet where possible?
options: The sheet will not spring back at all once it is bent
The metal is less likely to crack on the outside of the bend
The bend needs less force, so no machine is needed
The bend line is easier to see on the shiny surface

questions.stem: Which metal usually springs back the most after cold bending?
options: High-tensile or spring steel
Soft annealed copper
Soft lead sheet
Soft, fully annealed aluminium

questions.stem: What does annealing do to metal that has become hard from bending and hammering?
options: It hardens the metal further so that it keeps its shape
It coats the metal with zinc so that it does not rust
It softens it so it can be worked again without cracking
It polishes the metal so that it is ready for painting

questions.stem: A guillotine's rated capacity is given for which material?
options: Any metal at all, as long as the sheet fits under the blade
Aluminium; steel can be cut at the same thickness
The width of the sheet only, not its thickness
Mild steel; harder metals like stainless must be thinner

questions.stem: Which hand tool is best for cutting a curve to the left in 0.8 mm sheet steel?
options: Straight-cut snips
Bolt cutters
A cold chisel and hammer
Left-cut aviation snips

questions.stem: What should be done to cut edges before a part is folded or handled?
options: Paint them straight away to stop rust forming
Leave the burrs on, as they help the parts grip together
Remove the burrs with a file or a deburring tool
Hammer them flat with a heavy steel hammer

questions.stem: Which saw is best for cutting steel sections square to length?
options: A metal-cutting bandsaw or cold saw with the right blade
A circular saw with a blade made for cutting wood
A jigsaw fitted with a fine wood-cutting blade
A hand tile cutter with a hardened wheel

questions.stem: What is springback?
options: The metal cracking on the outside of the bend
The bend opening up a little when the force is removed
The sheet getting thinner along the bend line
The bend line slowly moving along the sheet as it is folded

questions.stem: During a bend, which part of the metal neither stretches nor squeezes?
options: The outside surface of the bend
The inside surface of the bend
The neutral axis, near the middle of the thickness
The two cut edges at each end of the bend line

questions.stem: What can happen if the inside bend radius is too small for the thickness of the metal?
options: The bend will be too weak to hold any paint
The outside of the bend may crack
The sheet will get thicker on the outside
The machine will bend it much more slowly

questions.stem: Which machine is used to make neat folds along the edges of sheet metal boxes and trays?
options: A box and pan folder (pan brake)
A pedestal grinder with a fine wheel
A pillar drill with a large vice
A power hacksaw with a clamp

questions.stem: Why are the corners of a sheet metal tray notched before folding?
options: So that the tray is lighter and cheaper to make
So that rust cannot form in the corners later
So that the folds can be made in any order without marking
So the sides fold up without bulging or overlapping

questions.stem: On a press brake, what forms the bend?
options: Two rolls turning against each other
A punch pressing the sheet into a die
A flame heating the line until it bends
A hammer striking the sheet on an anvil

questions.stem: When marking out a part to be bent, what is the bend allowance?
options: The extra length added at each end for welding
The gap left between two parts when they are fitted
The time allowed on the job card for the bending
The length of metal used up in the curved part of the bend

questions.stem: Why are the ends of a plate pre-bent before rolling it into a cylinder?
options: To make the plate softer before it is fed into the rolls
To mark the place where the seam weld will be made
The rolls leave the ends flat unless they are bent first
To stop the plate slipping out of the rolls halfway

questions.stem: A cylinder is to be rolled from 6 mm plate to an outside diameter of 500 mm. Which diameter is used to work out the length of plate?
options: 494 mm, the mean diameter
500 mm, the outside diameter
488 mm, the inside diameter
506 mm, outside plus thickness

questions.stem: The mean diameter of a cylinder is 300 mm. About how long must the plate be to roll it?
options: About 942 mm
About 600 mm
About 900 mm
About 1200 mm

questions.stem: How can you check the roundness of a rolled cylinder?
options: Lay a spirit level along the seam and read the bubble
Roll it along the floor and listen for any knocking
Use a curved template, or measure several diameters
Push a feeler gauge between the edges of the seam

questions.stem: On bending rolls, how is a tighter (smaller) curve made?
options: By feeding the plate through faster
By setting the rolls tighter a little at each pass
By heating the rolls with a gas torch before rolling
By one pass through at full pressure

questions.stem: When bending a steel pipe hot, why is it first packed tightly with dry sand?
options: To keep the inside of the pipe cool while it is heated
To make the pipe heavier so it stays still in the bender
To clean the rust off the inside wall as it bends
To support the walls so the pipe does not flatten or kink

questions.stem: Why must the sand used for hot pipe bending be completely dry?
options: Wet sand is too heavy to pour into the pipe easily
Wet sand makes the inside of the pipe rust quickly
Wet sand stops the heat getting through the wall
Water turns to steam and can blow the end plug out

questions.stem: When bending a pipe that has a welded seam, where should the seam be placed?
options: At the side, in line with the neutral axis of the bend
On the outside of the bend, where it can be seen
On the inside of the bend, where it is squeezed
Anywhere, because the seam makes no difference

questions.stem: What is one advantage of hot bending a thick steel bar instead of cold bending it?
options: The finished bar is always harder and stronger than before
Less force is needed and the bend is less likely to crack
No measuring or marking out is needed before bending
There is no need to wear gloves or other PPE

questions.stem: Which tool is best for forming thin sheet without denting or stretching it?
options: A ball-pein hammer
A heavy club or sledge hammer
A rawhide or wooden mallet
A centre punch and hammer

questions.stem: What is a hem (safe edge) on sheet metal?
options: A row of rivets placed along the edge of the sheet
The edge ground to a sharp, clean bevel for welding
The edge folded back flat on itself to stiffen it
A line scribed near the edge to show where to cut

questions.stem: What does hollowing (sinking) do to sheet metal?
options: Thickens it at the edges to make a strong rim
Cuts a round hole out of the middle of the sheet
Joins two sheets together with a folded seam
Stretches and thins it to form a dish shape

questions.stem: Why is a wire rolled inside the edge of a sheet metal job (a wired edge)?
options: To stiffen the edge and make it safe to handle
To carry electricity along the edge of the job
To give a place to hang the job up when painting
To mark the finished size of the job for checking

questions.stem: Why are parts tack welded before they are fully welded?
options: To make the full weld stronger by heating the parts first
To hold them in place so they can be checked and adjusted
To use up short welding rods left from other jobs
To test that the welding machine is working properly

questions.stem: Which method helps to reduce distortion when welding a fabricated frame?
options: Weld one side fully before tacking the other side
Clamp it in a jig and weld in a balanced order
Use the biggest weld possible on every joint
Cool each weld quickly with a wet rag or water

questions.stem: How can you check that a rectangular frame is square?
options: Measure both diagonals; they should be equal
Measure two opposite sides; they should be equal
Check one corner with the end of a tape measure
Look along the frame by eye from one end

questions.stem: When are pop (blind) rivets most useful for joining sheet metal?
options: When the joint must hold high pressure without leaking
When the parts must be taken apart again many times
When the metal is more than 25 mm thick
When you can reach only one side of the job

questions.stem: Which tool is used to check that a bend is 90°?
options: A set of feeler gauges
A centre punch
An engineer's square
A scriber and steel rule

questions.stem: A drawing says 200 ± 1 mm. Which measured size is acceptable?
Before changing tooling or clearing a jam on a machine, what must you do?
options: Run it slowly with the guard open so you can see
Ask someone to stand by the stop button while you work
Switch it off and isolate (lock off) the power supply
Keep it running but keep your hands well back

questions.stem: What should be done with offcuts and scrap sheet at the end of a job?
options: Leave them on the floor for the cleaner to sweep up
Stack them against the machines until they are needed
Throw them in the general rubbish with the paper waste
Sort them into the offcut and scrap bins, off the floor

questions.stem: A bending roll makes a grinding noise and the plate starts to slip. What should you do?
options: Feed the plate faster so it grips the rolls better
Stop, isolate the machine and report it to the instructor
Pour some oil onto the rolls while they are turning
Keep rolling the plate, but stand further back from the machine

questions.stem: What is a jig used for in fabrication?
options: Holding parts in place so each one is assembled the same
Lifting heavy plates from the steel rack onto the bench
Measuring the thickness of sheet and plate before cutting
Cutting curved shapes in thin sheet metal

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the shaped steel block, held in the bench, that sheet metal is formed over by hand?
What hammer, with a smooth polished face, is used to smooth out the marks on formed sheet metal?
What number, about 3.142, is multiplied by the mean diameter to find the length of plate for a cylinder?
A 3 mm sheet is bent with an inside radius of 3 mm. If the neutral axis is in the middle of the thickness, what is its radius in mm?
What is the name for metal becoming harder and more brittle as it is bent or hammered cold?
What is the name for the flat piece of sheet, cut to size and shape, before it is folded or rolled?
What machine rolls angle iron or flat bar into rings?
What hand tool is used with a hammer to close and lock down a folded (grooved) seam?
What is the name of the steel section shaped like a capital U or C?
What is the name of the steel section shaped like a capital L?
What is the name for an edge of sheet or plate bent up at 90° to stiffen it?
What machine cuts shapes in sheet metal by punching out many small bites?
What is the large red button that stops a machine at once called?
What is the name of the shaped block that a pipe is bent around in a pipe bender?
What hand tool, like wide flat-jawed pliers, is used to bend or fold a sheet edge by hand?

essays.stem: Describe how to use a guillotine safely to cut sheet metal, including the checks you make before, during and after cutting.
essays.modelAnswer: Before cutting, make sure you are trained and allowed to use the machine. Check that the guards and hold-downs are in place and working, the blade is in good order, and the sheet is within the rated capacity for that metal. The rating is for mild steel, so stainless steel must be thinner. Set the back gauge to the size needed and check it with a rule. Wear safety boots, gloves and safety glasses. During cutting, keep your fingers out of the guard and away from the hold-downs and the blade. Only one person works the foot pedal, and only when everyone's hands are clear. Support large sheets with a helper or a roller stand, and never reach behind the machine while it can operate. Do not cut rod, wire or anything the machine is not made for. After cutting, take the pieces out carefully because the edges are sharp, deburr them and stack them. Switch off and isolate the machine, clear the offcuts and report any fault.
markingPoints: Before: trained, guards and hold-downs in place, blade condition, sheet within the rated capacity (rated for mild steel)
Back gauge set and checked; PPE worn (boots, gloves, glasses)
During: hands clear of the guard, hold-downs and blade; one person only on the pedal
Large sheets supported; never reach behind the machine
After: careful handling and deburring, machine isolated, area cleared, faults reported

essays.stem: Explain how to plan a fabrication job from a drawing, up to the point where you are ready to start cutting.
essays.modelAnswer: Read the whole drawing first: the title block, the scale, the material, the views, the sizes and the notes, and check that it is the latest issue. Ask the supervisor about anything that is not clear. List every part on a cutting list with its size, material, thickness and the number needed, and allow for cutting and bending. Check that the material in the store is the right type and size and is not damaged. Work out the order of work, for example cut, deburr, mark out the bend lines, notch, bend or roll, then assemble and tack. Choose the machines and tools for each step, and check that they can handle the thickness and size, such as the guillotine and press brake ratings. Do a risk assessment for the job, looking at sharp edges, heavy lifting, machine nips and noise. Collect the PPE, clamps and jigs, and make sure the work area is clear before starting.
markingPoints: Reads the whole drawing and checks it is the current issue; asks about anything unclear
Makes a cutting list with sizes, materials, quantities and allowances
Checks the material is right and undamaged
Plans the order of work and chooses machines and tools within their capacity
Risk assessment, PPE and a clear work area

essays.stem: Explain what affects the amount of springback in a bend, and describe two ways a fabricator makes sure the finished bend is at the right angle.
essays.modelAnswer: Springback is the small amount a bend opens up after the force is taken off, because part of the metal behaves like a spring. It depends on the type of metal: harder and higher-strength metals, such as high-tensile or stainless steel, spring back more than mild steel, and soft copper or aluminium spring back less. A large bend radius gives more springback than a tight radius, and thinner material bent to the same radius also tends to spring back more. Metal that has been work hardened springs back more too. The fabricator allows for it by over-bending: bending a little past the angle needed so that it springs back to the right angle. The amount is found from experience, from the machine maker's tables, or from a test bend on an offcut of the same material. On a press brake the sheet can also be pressed fully into the die (bottoming), which reduces springback. Each bend is checked with a protractor or angle gauge and corrected before going on.
markingPoints: Springback explained: the bend opens a little when the force is removed
Harder or higher-strength metal springs back more than mild steel or soft metals
A larger radius (and thinner sheet for the same radius) gives more springback
Over-bending, judged from tables, experience or a test bend on an offcut
Bottoming on the press brake, and checking each bend with a protractor or gauge

essays.stem: Describe the steps to mark out, notch and fold a small open sheet metal tray on a box and pan folder.
essays.modelAnswer: Read the drawing and work out the size of the blank: the base length and width plus the height of each side, with an allowance for any hem. Cut the blank square on the guillotine and deburr it. Mark the bend lines with a scriber or fine marker, measuring from one datum edge. Mark the corner notches where the bend lines cross, and cut them out with snips so that the sides will fold up without overlapping or bulging. A small relief at the inside corner helps to stop tearing. If there are hems, fold these first while the sheet is still flat. Set the folder's clamp fingers to suit the base, line the bend line up with the clamping edge, clamp down, and lift the folding leaf to just past 90° to allow for springback. Fold two opposite sides first, then reset the fingers to fit between them and fold the other two sides. Check the sides with a square and the sizes with a rule, then finish the corners as the drawing shows.
markingPoints: Blank size worked out (base plus sides and hems), cut square and deburred
Bend lines marked from a datum; corner notches marked and cut, with a relief
Hems folded first while the sheet is flat
Folder fingers set, bend line lined up and clamped; folded just past 90° for springback
Opposite sides folded in order, then checked with a square and rule

essays.stem: Describe how to roll a cylinder from plate on three-roll bending rolls, from working out the length of the plate to checking the finished cylinder.
essays.modelAnswer: First work out the length of plate. Find the mean diameter, which is the outside diameter minus the plate thickness, or the inside diameter plus the thickness. Multiply the mean diameter by π (about 3.142). For example, a cylinder 500 mm outside diameter in 6 mm plate has a mean diameter of 494 mm, so the plate must be about 1552 mm long. Cut the plate square so that the seam will line up, and deburr it. Pre-bend both ends, on the press brake or in the rolls, because the rolls leave a flat on each end. Feed the plate in square to the rolls, and tighten them a little at each pass so the curve is made over several passes, never all at once. Keep hands and clothing clear of the nip and work the controls from the safe side. Check the curve often with a template cut to the right radius. When the edges meet, check the gap and line-up, tack the seam, and check the roundness by measuring the diameter in several places.
markingPoints: Length = mean diameter × π (mean = outside diameter − thickness, or inside + thickness), with a correct example
Plate cut square and deburred; ends pre-bent to avoid flats
Plate fed square; rolls tightened a little each pass over several passes
Hands kept clear of the nip; curve checked with a template
Seam lined up and tacked; roundness checked by measuring several diameters

essays.stem: Describe how to bend a steel pipe to 90° with a pipe bender, and explain the faults that can happen and how to prevent them.
essays.modelAnswer: Check the drawing for the bend angle, the radius and where the bend starts. Choose a former and guide that match the pipe's outside diameter, because the wrong size will crush the pipe. Mark the start of the bend on the pipe. If the pipe has a welded seam, turn it so the seam is at the side, on the neutral axis, not on the inside or outside of the bend. Put the pipe in the bender, line the mark up with the start of the former, and bend slowly and steadily, a little past 90° to allow for springback. Check the angle with a square or protractor. Common faults are flattening (the pipe goes oval), kinking, wrinkling on the inside of the bend and splitting on the outside. They are prevented by using the right former and guide, not bending tighter than the smallest radius for that pipe, bending steadily, and supporting the pipe walls. For hot or very tight bends the pipe can be packed with dry sand. Wear gloves and keep fingers clear of the former.
markingPoints: Former and guide matched to the pipe outside diameter; bend start marked
Seam placed at the side (neutral axis)
Bent slowly and steadily, slightly past 90° for springback, then the angle checked
Faults named: flattening, kinking, wrinkling, splitting
Prevention: correct former, not below the minimum radius, steady bending, wall support (dry sand for hot bends)

essays.stem: Compare hot forming and cold forming of steel. Give an advantage and a disadvantage of each, and an example of when you would use each.
essays.modelAnswer: Cold forming is shaping the steel at room temperature with machines or hand tools, for example folding sheet on a pan brake, rolling plate or bending flat bar in a bender. Its advantages are a clean finish with no scale, accurate and repeatable sizes, and no fire or burn hazards. Its disadvantages are that it needs more force, the metal work hardens and may crack on tight bends, and there is springback. Cold forming suits sheet metal work, light sections and most repeat jobs. Hot forming is shaping the steel after heating it, usually to a bright red, with an oxy-fuel torch or a furnace. Its advantages are that much less force is needed, thick bars and sections can be bent, and the metal is less likely to crack. Its disadvantages are scale on the surface, sizes that are harder to control, possible distortion, and burn and fire hazards. Hot forming suits thick bar, heavy sections and one-off bends, such as bending a 25 mm round bar into a hook for a gate.
markingPoints: Cold forming explained, with an advantage (clean, accurate, no heat hazard)
A disadvantage of cold forming (more force, work hardening, cracking, springback)
Hot forming explained, with an advantage (less force, thick sections, less cracking)
A disadvantage of hot forming (scale, less accuracy, distortion, burns and fire)
A sensible example of when to use each

essays.stem: Describe three hand forming methods for sheet metal, such as hollowing, raising, planishing or wiring an edge, and the tools used for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Hollowing (sinking) makes a shallow dish. The sheet is hammered from the inside into a hollow in a wooden block or a sandbag, using a round-faced bossing mallet or hollowing hammer, working in circles from the outside edge towards the centre. The metal stretches and gets thinner. Raising makes a deeper shape, such as a bowl, by hammering the sheet from the outside over a stake, working round in rings from the base outwards. The metal is squeezed in and stays about the same thickness or gets a little thicker. Planishing smooths out the bumps left by hollowing or raising. The work is held on a polished stake that matches its shape and struck with light, even blows of a planishing hammer, which has a smooth, polished face. Wiring an edge stiffens it and makes it safe. The edge is turned round a wire with a mallet on a hatchet stake, or in a wiring machine, and closed tightly. Metal that becomes hard while being worked is annealed to soften it again.
markingPoints: Hollowing: hammered into a hollow block or sandbag with a bossing mallet; metal stretches and thins
Raising: hammered over a stake from the outside in rings; metal is squeezed in
Planishing: light, even blows of a planishing hammer on a polished stake
Wiring: edge turned round a wire with a mallet on a stake, or in a machine
Correct tools named for each method described (annealing when the metal hardens)

essays.stem: Explain how to assemble and tack weld a rectangular steel frame so that it is square, flat and has little distortion.
essays.modelAnswer: Check that all the members are cut to the right length with clean, square or mitred ends, and deburr them. Lay the parts out on a flat welding table or level trestles, against stops or in a jig, with clamps to hold them in place. Check that the joints fit closely with even gaps. Tack one corner, then check it with a square before tacking the others. When all the corners are tacked, measure both diagonals. If they are not equal, push the frame along the longer diagonal until they match. Check that the frame lies flat on the table. Add more tacks on each joint, placed evenly on both sides. For the full welding, keep the frame clamped and weld in a balanced order, for example opposite corners in turn, using short runs rather than one long run so the heat is spread out. Check the diagonals and flatness again after welding and while it cools.
markingPoints: Parts cut, ends square and deburred; laid out flat in a jig or against stops and clamped
Good fit-up with even gaps; first corner tacked and checked with a square
Diagonals measured and made equal; frame checked flat
Tacks placed evenly; frame kept clamped for welding
Balanced welding order with short runs; checked again after welding

essays.stem: Describe how you would check a finished fabricated part against its drawing, finish it, and what you would do if it is outside tolerance.
essays.modelAnswer: Check the drawing for the sizes, angles and tolerances, and use measuring tools that are in good order: a steel rule and tape, an engineer's square, a protractor, radius gauges and templates. Measure the overall sizes, the positions of holes and bends, the bend angles and the radius of any rolled parts, and compare each one with the drawing and its tolerance. Check that rolled parts are round, that frames are square by measuring the diagonals, and that flat parts are flat with a straight edge. Look over the whole part for burrs, sharp edges, dents, cracks at the bends and weld faults. Finish it by removing burrs and sharp edges, grinding welds where the drawing asks, and cleaning off oil and scale ready for painting. Write the results on the job card. If a size is outside tolerance, do not hide it or pass it on. Mark the part, tell the supervisor or instructor, and agree whether it can be reworked, for example by rebending, or must be made again.
markingPoints: Measures each size, angle and position against the drawing and its tolerance, with suitable tools
Checks squareness, flatness and roundness
Looks for burrs, cracks, dents and weld faults
Finishes: deburrs, removes sharp edges, cleans ready for painting; records the results
Outside tolerance: marks it, reports to the supervisor, reworks or remakes as agreed

practical1.title: Mark out, notch and fold a sheet metal tray with hemmed edges
practical1.brief: Each member of the group makes one open tray from 0.8–1.0 mm mild steel or galvanised sheet: base 150 mm × 100 mm, sides 25 mm high, square notched corners, and a 6 mm hem along the top edge of each long side. The group shares the machines and takes turns, but every member does every step on their own tray: works out and marks the blank size, cuts it on the guillotine under the instructor's eye, deburrs it, marks the bend lines, cuts the corner notches with snips, folds the hems and then the sides on the box and pan folder, and checks the sizes and angles. Label each tray with the member's name. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every tray is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 0.8–1.0 mm mild steel or galvanised sheet, about 220 mm × 180 mm for each member
Guillotine and box and pan folder
Scriber or fine marker, steel rule, engineer's square and protractor
The tray drawing, and name labels
photos: Each member's blank, marked out with bend lines and corner notches
The corner notches cut and the edges deburred
A hem being folded on the folder
A side being folded, with the member's hands clear of the clamp
Each finished tray checked with a square and rule
All the finished trays together, with name labels
The work area cleaned, with offcuts in the bins
checklist: Wore gloves, safety glasses and boots, and handled the sheet safely
Worked out the blank size correctly and marked the bend lines from a datum edge
Used the guillotine safely, with hands clear and under supervision
Cut clean corner notches and removed all burrs
Folded the hems flat and the sides to 90° (within about 2°), with hands clear of the folder
Finished tray is within ±1 mm of the drawing sizes, with no bulged or torn corners
Left the machines and area clean, with offcuts sorted
safety: Wear gloves when handling sheet; the edges and burrs are sharp
Only one person works the guillotine pedal; keep fingers out of the guard and away from the hold-downs
Keep fingers clear of the folder clamp and leaf; never reach in while someone else is working it
Isolate machines before adjusting or clearing them; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Keep the floor clear of offcuts

practical2.title: Roll and tack a cylinder from 2 mm sheet, and cold-bend a flat bar to 90°
practical2.brief: As a group, work out the blank length for a cylinder 200 mm outside diameter and 150 mm long in 2 mm mild steel sheet (mean diameter × π), and show the working on a card. Mark out and cut the blank square, and pre-bend both ends. Roll the cylinder on the bending rolls: every member makes at least one rolling pass while the assessor watches, and checks the curve with a template the group makes from thin sheet or card. Close the seam, check the gap and line-up, and tack it in the welding bay under supervision, with members taking turns to hold, check and tack. Then every member cold-bends a 25 mm × 6 mm mild steel flat bar to 90° at a marked line in a bar bender, allowing for springback, and checks it with a square. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: 2 mm mild steel sheet, about 650 mm × 160 mm
Bending rolls rated for 2 mm sheet
Thin sheet or card for a 100 mm radius template
Guillotine, files, steel rule, tape and scriber
Welding set for tacking, with welding PPE and screens
25 mm × 6 mm mild steel flat bar, 300 mm long, one for each member
Bar bender, engineer's square and protractor
photos: The group's working for the blank length, on a card
The blank marked out and cut square
A member making a rolling pass, with hands clear of the rolls
The template held against the cylinder
The seam tacked, and the diameter being measured

Bent the flat bar to 90° (within about 2°) at the mark, allowing for springback
Left the machines isolated and the area clean
safety: Keep hands, gloves and loose clothing away from the nip of the rolls; know where the stop button is
Two people handle long sheet; the edges are sharp
Tack only in the welding bay or behind screens, with full welding PPE
Keep fingers clear of the bar bender's former; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Isolate machines before adjusting or clearing them
